v.why: The direct shortcut makes the extra conv path redundant.
Shortcut redundancy reduces the benefit of upgrading the stem edge.
The shortcut already gives the output node an easy gradient path.
The skip aids trainability so the 0->2 conv can carry the main feature path.
Removing the direct edge costs less when conv capacity is redundant elsewhere, so the accuracy change is higher (less negative).
A skip already provides identity flow so a 1x1 conv adds little.
Diminishing returns on stacked receptive field when the upstream edge is already a 3x3 conv.
Path 0->1->3 already has enough capacity from the upstream conv.
Node 2 already gets rich features so a 1x1 adds little.
Stacking pooling on both output paths loses information.

raw:
I dropped the hypotheses that mostly restate "removing a path makes the remaining ones matter more" (edit 1 conv3x3 | edge 0 none, edit 0 conv1x1 | edge 1 none, edit 3 skip | edge 4 none). I also dropped the ones whose direction most practitioners would predict, such as upgrading pooling to a conv, or replacing the stem conv with a skip. The ten below rest on redundancy, saturation, or optimization-ease mechanisms, with directions that are less obvious. They are ranked by judgment, not tested against benchmark data.
